2 2.

As per the complaint, on 23.11.2007, the food officials including Food Inspector (FI) Sanjeev Kumar Gupta and Field Assistant (FA) Brahmanand under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Ranjeet Singh reached at the premises of accused no. 5 M/s. K.M.
Enterprises (partnership firm) at D-3, Progressive Chamber, D- Block, Central Market, Prashant Vihar, Delhi-110085, where the accused no. 1 in the capacity of its vendor-cum-partner was found conducting the business of various food articles, including 'Kitchen King', which was found stored for sale for human consumption, lying in sealed packets of 100 gm each bearing identical label declaration.
The food officials lifted the sample the said food article consisting of 9 such sealed packets of Kitchen King ready for sale.
It was divided into three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules and separately packed and sealed.
Necessary documents were prepared at the spot including the vendor's receipt and panchanama.
Price of the sample was paid to the vendor.
One counterpart of the sample was deposited with the Public Analyst (PA) and remaining two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated 27.12.2007, the PA reported that the article was conforming to the standards, yet the sample was found misbranded being in violation of Rule 37A(2) of PFA Rules, because it was without declaration of name of food or category under which it fell.
Based on the report of PA, investigation was carried out by the Food Inspector as per the instructions of the SDM/LHA.

At the time of sampling, the accused no. 1 vendor had disclosed that the commodity had been supplied to him by M/s. Dalmia INC alias Manglam Traders (Proprietorship concern of accused no. 6), which had intern purchased it from M/s R.R.
Enterprises (proprietorship concern of accused no.7).
Investigation revealed that accused no. 5 firm had four partners (accused no. 1 to 4 herein), all of whom were implicated in the matter.

Further,
the food article had been supplied to the distributor accused no. 7 by accused no. 10 partnership firm, of which accused no. 8 and 9 were the partners.
The food article had been manufactured by accused no. 12 company, of which accused no. 11 had been appointed as nominee under Section 17 of PFA Act.

Hence, after obtaining due sanction of the Director, PFA, the present complaint came to be filed against all the accused persons for violation of the section 2(ix)(k) read with Rule 37A(2) of PFA Rules, as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act for selling /distributing /
manufacturing misbranded food.
3. Since the complaint was filed by a public servant in writing, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 02.07.2008.

Based on the report of PA, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed vide order dated 17.03.2010 against all the accused persons for commission of offence under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
4. At the trial, the prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.
PW-1 Sh. Ranjeet Singh, PW-2 FI Sanjeev Kumar Gupta and PW-3 FI Raj Pal Singh were examined.
PW-1 and PW-2 were a part of the team that had visited the premises of accused no. 5 (where accused no. 1 was the vendor) and lifted the sample of Kitchen King lying in sealed packets of 100 gm each.

These witnesses deposed about the sample proceedings conducted by them on 23.11.2007 and narrated the steps undertaken by them, including disclosing their identity, lifting of 9 sealed packets of 100 gm each, dividing the same in three counterparts by putting 3 sealed packets as one counterpart and separately packing them.
A sum of Rs.270/- was offered to the vendor as price of the sample vide vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A but the same was refused on the ground that the food article was not In Re vs A-1)

Sh. Hitesh Khatuja on 15 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144812211/
3 for sale and was used only for preparation of other food articles.
Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C were prepared at the spot.
Based on the information given by the accused no. 1, notice under section 14A of PFA Act, Ex. PW-1/D was prepared addressed to accused no. 6.
One counterpart was deposited with the PA vide receipt Ex. PW-1/F and remaining two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA vide receipt Ex.
PW-1 /
E. PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received opining the sample to be misbranded.

Further investigation was carried out during which letters were written to the vendor, distributor, supplier, manufacturer and Government departments so as to ascertain their roles and involvement and their replies received.
The said communications are Ex. PW-2/A to Ex. PW-2/H.
Further investigation was carried out by PW-3 who also wrote letter Ex. PW-3/A to the STO and received reply Ex. PW-3/B.

After completion of investigation, consent for prosecution Ex. PW-3/C was taken from the Director, PFA, after which the complaint Ex.
PW-3/D was filed and intimation letter Ex. PW- 3/E was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-3/F. Vide order dated 14.09.2011,
Ld. Defence Counsel admitted the role of FA upon which he was discharged unexamined and PE was closed.
5. PW-1 during cross-examination accepted that the samples were sealed and that the list of ingredients was also mentioned on the product.
He went on to accept that Kitchen King was a popular name for Masala.
PW-2 during cross-examination affirmed this fact, though he could not say if Kitchen King was popular name of Masala.
PW-3 was not cross examined by Ld. Defence Counsel.
6. In the meanwhile, vide order dated 20.04.2012, the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi quashed the proceedings against accused no. 9.
Subsequently, several applications were moved under Section 294 CrPC which were disposed of vide order dated 11.09.2013 and the accused no. 1 to 6 were discharged.
Record shows that similar applications were moved by accused no. 7 and 8 and the matter was listed for arguments on the applications.
Order dated 18.11.2014 shows no objection of Ld. Counsel for accused no. 12, 10 and 8 if benefit of warranty was granted to the said applicants.
However, no further orders were passed on the applications.

7. Statements of the accused no.7,8 (also representing accused no. 10) and 11 (also representing accused no.12) were recorded under section 313 CrPC on 04.04.2015 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
They expressed ignorance of sample proceedings on the ground that they were not present at that time.
Accused no
. 7 claimed that he had purchased the food article from accused no. 8 and had sold it in the same condition as purchased.
Accused no. 8 and 10 also maintained that the food article had been procured from accused no. 12 and had supplied it in the same condition.
Accused no. 12 and its nominee accused no. 11 disputed the PA report on the ground that there was nothing to mislead any customer and that there was no violation of any rule.
No defence evidence was however led by them despite opportunity.

8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to prove its case against all the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt, as all the witnesses have supported its case and there is no condition in their testimony.
It is submitted that the accused persons have failed to rebut the findings as given by the PA.

In Re vs A-1) Sh. Hitesh Khatuja on 15 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144812211/
4 9.
On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons has submitted that the prosecution case fails on technical grounds.
Ld. Counsel submits that there is no violation of any rule including Rule 37A(2) of PFA Rules as the name "Kitchen King" is a trade name of masala which is recognized by this name only.
It is submitted that the food article was a proprietary food and all its ingredients had been mentioned on the label and therefore, no customer was misled in any manner.
10. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons and have carefully perused the material available on record.
11. In a criminal trial, the burden is on the complainant / prosecution to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and has to be necessarily discharged by the prosecution itself by leading cogent and trustworthy evidence.
12. To begin with, it is seen that the accused persons have not disputed the factum of lifting of sample from the premises of accused no. 5 on 23.11.2007.
It is not their case that no such proceedings took place or that no such food article was exposed / stored / meant for use in preparation of food articles meant for sale for human consumption.
Both the PW-1 and PW-2 have deposed about the sample proceedings and have narrated the steps undertaken by them in detail and in corroboration to each other.
It is not disputed that the food officials had lifted 9 sealed packets of 100 gm each of food article bearing identical label declaration.
Both the said PWs, who were a part of the team that had lifted the sample, have deposed in corroboration of each other.
No contradiction at all can be seen in their testimony that could go to the root of the matter so as to disbelieve them.
They all deposed about steps undertaken by them during sample proceedings.
All deposed about compliance of rules while lifting the sample.
No question or suggestion was put to them regarding non- compliance of any mandatory rule.
All the witnesses deposed that attempt was made to join public persons as witnesses but none had joined.
There is nothing to disbelieve them or to shake their credibility.
Their cross- examination was confined to a very limited extent.
13. It is then not in dispute that the food article had been manufactured by accused no. 12 company.

The label declarations and the documents on record would show that the food article was manufactured / packed by this company, of which accused no. 11 had been appointed as nominee and deemed to be incharge and responsible to the company for its affairs.

14. The accused persons have also not questioned the analytical values in the PA report Ex. PW-1/G,
though they have questioned her opinion as to violation of PFA Rule.

It is nowhere the stand of the accused persons that the said report is wrong or any incorrect method had been applied by the PA,
primarily because the said report is in their favour in as much as the sample was found conforming to the prescribed standards as to its nature, quality and substance.
15.

The only question is if the food article can be said to be "without declaration of name of food or category under which it falls", as observed by the PA on the basis of which the sample was opined to be misbranded being in violation of Rule 37A(2) of PFA Rules.

In Re vs A-1) Sh. Hitesh Khatuja on 15 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144812211/
5 16.
Rule 37A of PFA Rules deals with proprietary food which has not been standardized under PFA Rules.
Thus, all the food articles which do not fall in any of the items mentioned in Appendix-B of PFA Rules, are treated as proprietary food articles.

Since no standards have been prescribed nor can be prescribed for such food articles which have not been standardized, the manufacturer is free to prepare them as per his own ingredients or mode or manner, provided that the same is not in violation of PFA Rules.

Rule 37A(2) of PFA Rules provides that in addition to the labelling requirement, the proprietary food articles shall also conform to certain requirements like, obtaining separate licences by the manufacturer / halwais, mentioning of name of food and / or category under which it falls on the label, prohibition of use of tobacco and nicotine, use of only permitted food additives, etc.
17.

In the present case, it is submitted that the food article in question did not mention the name of the food and / or category under which it fell on its label, as required by Rule 37A(2)(b).
18.
The main label declarations had been reproduced by the FI on Form VI Ex. PW-1/B, the correctness of which has not been disputed by the defence.
It shows that the food article was stated as "Kitchen King" being sold under the brand name MDH.
There was compliance of labelling rules including Rule 32 as lot number, date of packing, best before date, MRP, name of manufacturer and list of ingredients had been duly mentioned on the label.
It is thus to be ascertained if "Kitchen King" can be called as name of the food article or category under which it fell.
19. The words "name of the food" or "category" have not been defined in PFA Act or Rules.

However,
Rule 32(b)(1) specifies that the name of the food shall include trade name or description of food contained in the package.
The stand of the accused persons is that "Kitchen King" is a trade name being commonly used by the consumers.

20. In this regard, it is pertinent to note that when the sample was lifted by the food officials, there was no doubt in their mind about the nature, identity or category of food which was lifted by them.

The vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, Notice Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex.PW-1/C, Notice Ex.PW- 1/D,
which were prepared at the spot by the FI himself clearly mention the name of the food article as "Kitchen King Masala".
At all the places where the name of the food is to be mentioned on these documents, the FI mentioned the Kitchen King to be a masala.
Further, the list of ingredients mentioned on the label would also show the nature of food article which is an admixture of several powdered spices and condiments.
21. There is nothing to show that FI had any doubt on the day of sampling as to the nature or identity or name of the food article or the category under which it fell.
Till that day, it was not the case of the food officials that the proprietary food being lifted by them could not be identified or its name /category could not be ascertained.
It has not been explained as to why and how the FI mentioned the food article to be a masala, when the label never declared the food article to be masala.

The very fact that the FI identified the food article to be masala, would show that even from the name of the food article as given on the label, that is, "Kitchen King", it was clear that it was a masala.

None of documents prepared at the spot bear any endorsement to the effect that the food article could not be identified or its name / category was unascertainable or that it was being In Re vs A-1) Sh. Hitesh Khatuja on 15 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144812211/
6 considered as masala only on the basis of the version of the vendor, as claimed by the FI in his complaint.

It was only after the PA report was received that the FI got the wisdom and he mentioned in the complaint that the vendor had referred the food article as "Kitchen King Masala" while writing his statement on the vendor's receipt and Form VI so the FI incorporated the word "masala"
in the name of the sampled commodity while preparing the sample documents.
Apparently, such a version is an afterthought.
The endorsement by the vendor on Ex. PW-1/A and Ex. PW-1/B was made only subsequent to the preparation of these documents.
The contents of these documents were first filled by the FI and the endorsements thereupon were made by the vendor only thereafter.
Therefore, it would not be correct for the FI to claim that he mentioned the food article as "Kitchen King Masala" only on the basis of the endorsements of the vendor.
It is rather apparent that the food officials were clear that Kitchen King was a masala and therefore, they mentioned it to be "Kitchen King Masala".
This fact was confirmed by both PW-1 and PW-2 during their cross-examination.
22. Further, PW-1 categorically accepted that Kitchen King was a popular name for masala, though PW-2 avoided to answer the same stated that he could not say to this effect.

When Kitchen King as a masala was treated as a proprietary food and not a standardized food, it cannot be said that there was no declaration of name of the food article or the category under which it fell.
It is not a case where there was absolute omission to mention the name of the food article.
Rather the food article was sold under the name "Kitchen King".
It is nowhere the case of the prosecution that the food article was being sold under a wrong name or under a misleading name.
When Kitchen King is known by its own name in common usage by the consumers, it can be safely called as the name of the product.
Such name can be a common name or trade name or generic name by which a product is identified by the ordinary consumers.
Further, the list of ingredients clearly show the contents of Kitchen King which would also remove any doubt as to the nature of food article.

23. In such position, it cannot be said that the food article was without declaration of name and / or category of food under which it fell so as to call it a violation of Rule 37A(2) of PFA Act, as opined by the PA.
Benefit of doubt has to be given to the accused persons on this count.

24. In view of this discussion, it can be said that the prosecution has not been able to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt that the accused persons had sold / distributed/ manufactured a misbranded food article.
25. Having said so, accused no. 7,8,10,11 and 12 are acquitted of the charges.
Bail bonds of accused no. 7,8 and 11 shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of Section 437A CrPC.
26. File be consigned to record room.
